plan.topic: Semaglutide (Ozempic) and chronic kidney disease in type 2 diabetes: what the randomized FLOW kidney-outcomes trial (NEJM 2024) found, what the US Ozempic label's kidney indication covers, what CKD and eGFR/urine albumin mean, the heart and survival secondary results, side effects and stopping rates, and questions to ask your doctor about kidney checks
plan.angle:
Evergreen explainer built on settled evidence, 9–11 min. Sources:
- FLOW, Perkovic et al., NEJM 2024 (PubMed): 3,533 adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, semaglutide vs placebo, median follow-up about 3.4 years, stopped early at a planned interim analysis for efficacy
- Ozempic US PI Section 1 and 6.1 (FDALabel effective 1 Jun 2026, version 20, Ozempic only; never borrow another label's date)
- NIDDK or NHS CKD pages for definitions, each with its own URL and live date

Opening:
- Sentence 1 names semaglutide (Ozempic), asks the title's question and answers it with a 'you' moment. Example: 'If you have type 2 diabetes and kidney disease: in a big randomized trial, fewer people on semaglutide had serious kidney events than on placebo.'
- Payoff at 15–30 s: the primary composite per arm as in the paper (about 18.7% vs 23.2%, HR 0.76), with the population on the card.
- Never say 'Short answer.', no list opening, no 'meet the trial' scene.

Chapters, named as searched questions:
1. What is CKD, and what are eGFR and urine albumin? Definitions from NIDDK or NHS.
2. What did FLOW find? The primary result and what the composite includes, exactly as the paper words it.
3. Heart and survival: secondary outcomes as printed with both arms. Say they're secondary.
4. What the US label says: quote Section 1's kidney indication word for word with its population. It's for adults with type 2 diabetes and CKD, not CKD without diabetes, and not shown for tirzepatide.
5. Side effects: serious adverse events 49.6% vs 53.8% as a whole-trial result. GI effects in label wording, and stopping because of adverse events per arm as printed. Always 'adverse events', never 'side effects', for trial figures.
6. Questions to ask your doctor: how often to check eGFR and urine albumin, and other medicines. Include the dehydration line in label wording, the low-blood-sugar caveat with insulin or a sulfonylurea, and the Medication Guide's emergency pancreatitis line verbatim, followed by the fixed don't-stop line.

Rules:
- No dose numbers, switching or stopping advice, and no 'now' or 'new'.
- 'Linked to' and 'may' wording kept exactly as the source has it. One result per sentence with its population.
- Lists of 3 items at most. Re-hook every 45–75 s. Land the last new fact before 80%. Never end a chapter on a warning card.
- One subscribe ask after the chapter 2 payoff.
- Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Post note watch-next target: Side Effects.
- Thumbnail: 'KIDNEYS TOO?' with one calm labelled character, no organ imagery.

package.description:
Not personal advice. Stop using Ozempic and call your health care provider right away if you have severe pain in your stomach area (abdomen) that will not go away, with or without vomiting. For anything that isn't that emergency sign, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

Quick answer: in the FLOW trial (NEJM 2024) of 3,533 adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, major kidney disease events occurred in 18.7% on semaglutide vs 23.2% on placebo over a median of about 3.4 years (HR 0.76). It does not cover CKD without diabetes.

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: First, the two numbers on Ray's letter.

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: Chronic kidney disease means your kidneys are damaged and cannot filter blood the way they should.

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: In the United States, diabetes is the leading cause of kidney disease, and high blood pressure also raises the risk.

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: About one in three adults with diabetes has kidney disease. At a table of six adults with diabetes, that would be two of them.

visual.stat_label: Adults with diabetes who have kidney disease

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: Early kidney disease may not cause any symptoms, which is exactly why the blood and urine tests matter.

visual.stock_query: person feeling fine, holding lab slip

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: The first number is eGFR, short for estimated glomerular filtration rate. It comes from a blood test and estimates how well your kidneys filter.

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: On the NIDDK scale, an eGFR of sixty or more is in the normal range, and below sixty may mean kidney disease.

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: On that same scale, an eGFR of fifteen or less is called kidney failure.

visual.stock_query: dial needle near low end, calm

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: The second number comes from urine. Albumin is a protein in your blood, and a healthy kidney does not let it pass into the urine.

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: A damaged kidney lets some albumin leak through, which is why the urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio is checked.

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: A normal result is thirty milligrams per gram or less. More than thirty may be a sign of kidney disease.

visual.stock_query: lab cup icon with green check

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: Think of eGFR as how fast the filter works, and albumin as whether it is leaking.

visual.stock_query: coffee filter analogy, speed and drip

scenes.section: What is CKD? eGFR and urine albumin
scenes.narration: FLOW required both: raised urine albumin, plus an eGFR within set ranges between twenty-five and seventy-five.

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: The box counted kidney failure, meaning dialysis, a transplant, or an eGFR below fifteen.

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: It also counted a drop in eGFR of at least fifty percent from the start, or death from kidney-related or cardiovascular causes.

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: Out of three thousand five hundred thirty-three adults, three hundred thirty-one on semaglutide had a first event, versus four hundred ten on placebo.

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: Picture two rooms of one hundred trial participants: roughly nineteen with an event in the semaglutide room, about twenty-three in the placebo room.

visual.stock_query: two rooms of people, calm comparison

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: But a composite can hide which piece did the work. So here is the kidney-only part.

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: The kidney-specific parts of the composite had a hazard ratio of zero point seven nine versus placebo, so the kidney pieces also favored semaglutide.

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: And a secondary outcome tracked the slow slide in kidney function. The yearly eGFR decline was less steep by one point one six units with semaglutide than with placebo.

visual.stat_label: Less steep yearly eGFR decline, semaglutide vs placebo

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: Kidney disease can get worse over time, so a gentler slope each year is a number your doctor can follow across visits.

visual.stock_query: doctor and patient reviewing chart, smiling

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: For Ray, that is the translation he wanted: in adults like him, the trial found fewer major kidney disease events. A lower risk, not a cure.

scenes.section: What did the FLOW trial find?
scenes.narration: And it is one trial in one group: adults with type two diabetes and chronic kidney disease. It does not tell us about kidney disease without diabetes.

scenes.section: What does the Ozempic label say?

script.cta: One subscribe ask, after the chapter 2 payoff (s36): "If plain-language breakdowns of the big GLP-one trials help you, subscribe, so the next one finds you." Closing line, without contractions (s79): "There is a video I would watch next, linked in the description." POST NOTE, WATCH-NEXT TARGET: the channel's broad practical "Side Effects" long video, which is the "Side Effects" entry in the playbook's link list (new broad videos → Side Effects). The publisher must look up its exact live title and URL on the channel list and link that one video. Do not use the home page or a playlist, and never use the duplicate MQqAwUKAKSI. Drug match: no semaglutide (Ozempic) side-effects long video appears in the playbook or our analytics, and the Side Effects video covers tirzepatide. If a semaglutide (Ozempic) side-effects long video is live, link that instead, because it matches this video's drug. The copywriter leaves line 1 of the description empty, and the description ends "…whether it's right for you." Thumbnail: "KIDNEYS TOO?" with one calm, labelled character and no organ imagery. MOTION DESIGNER, fixed pre-split safety cards (never run them through the auto-splitter). s65 is exactly two cards. Card 1: "SEVERE STOMACH-AREA PAIN THAT WILL NOT GO AWAY, WITH OR WITHOUT VOMITING". Card 2: "STOP USING OZEMPIC AND CALL YOUR HEALTH CARE PROVIDER RIGHT AWAY". s66 is exactly two cards. Card 1: "FOR ANYTHING THAT ISN'T THAT EMERGENCY SIGN". Card 2: "DON'T STOP OR CHANGE YOUR MEDICINE ON YOUR OWN." Before handoff, check the transcript for "semaglutide", "Ozempic", "tirzepatide", "Mounjaro" and "Zepbound", and check every spoken "point" in the numbers.

factcheck.summary: Every factual claim checks out against primary sources. FLOW (NEJM 2024;391(2):109-121): 3,533 adults, median 3.4 yrs, stopped early for efficacy at a planned interim analysis, composite correctly described, 331 vs 410 first events (18.7% vs 23.2%), HR 0.76 / 24% lower, kidney-specific HR 0.79, CV death HR 0.71, MACE HR 0.82, all-cause death HR 0.80, eGFR slope 1.16 less steep, SAEs 49.6% vs 53.8%. The 13.2% vs 11.9% dropout figure was found in search results, not read in the paper. The Ozempic Section 1 indications (kidney use word for word) and the ≥5% adverse reactions match the label. The Medication Guide dehydration, drink-fluids, low blood sugar and pancreatitis wording matches. The NIDDK eGFR/UACR cut-offs, CKD definition, 1-in-3 figure and review dates (Oct 2016, Feb 2017, Feb 2025) are accurate. Framing is sound: relative and absolute numbers both given, supporting results labelled as such, scope kept to T2D + CKD, tirzepatide and CKD without diabetes excluded. Safety caveats are present. Only minor polish is needed.

thumbnail.reasoning: All three keep the answer hidden (no hard-cap violations) and match title tone. #0 is clean and on-brand with the Ozempic tag, but the blue-on-blue palette is similar to typical feed thumbnails. #1 uses a high-contrast purple background and a single bold black pill-silhouette-with-'?' focal point that will pop against a mostly blue/white YouTube feed, with crisp, large, legible text even at 168px — the strongest scroll-stopping curiosity gap with no clutter. #2's big number '3,533' is a nice credibility hook, but it crowds the frame with a worried pill face, magnifier icon, number and two text blocks, so the small 'T2D + CKD' tag and secondary text get cramped at phone size, slightly hurting legibility. #1 offers the best combination of CTR pull and clean legibility.
